CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches over the past few months with incidental discovery of pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male presenting for neurosurgical consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard regarding a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion. The patient initially presented to his primary care provider on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches. He denies any prior history of headaches. Workup with brain MRI and serology led to incidental discovery of a pituitary lesion. The headaches began approximately three months ago with gradual onset. Initial severity was 3/10, progressing to current severity of 6/10. Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull nagging ache, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. Patient reports no exacerbating or relieving factors. He additionally reports recently bumping into door frames but denies vision changes on direct questioning. He denies nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Patient tried acetaminophen without relief and discontinued.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies fever, rash, nausea, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or loss of consciousness. Denies vision changes on questioning. Denies weakness or balance problems. Recent eye exam in fall was normal per patient.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. No prior medical problems.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications. Tried acetaminophen for headaches without benefit.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient is adopted and reports no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a home. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use. Never used these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect appropriate, speech fluent. Cranial nerves grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficits in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive to light. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal.

RESULTS
CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal from 3/3/21. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH; all other results normal. Brain MRI with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign-appearing pituitary adenoma with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Patient is symptomatic with progressive headaches and bitemporal hemianopia. Surgical intervention via transsphenoidal approach indicated for excision and decompression of pituitary fossa. Risks of surgery discussed including anesthesia risks (myocardial infarction, stroke, death), infection, need for further surgery, cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficits, and death. Patient understands and consents to procedure. Will arrange surgery scheduling with surgery coordinator. Referral placed for preoperative visual field testing to assess peripheral vision and provide comparison for postoperative evaluation of vision improvement.
